title: Composite analysis with Monte Carlo methods: an example with cosmic rays and clouds

venue.name: Journal of Space Weather and Space Climate

abstract:
The composite (superposed epoch) analysis technique has been frequently
employed to examine a hypothesized link between solar activity and the Earth's
atmosphere, often through an investigation of Forbush decrease (Fd) events
(sudden high-magnitude decreases in the flux cosmic rays impinging on the
upper-atmosphere lasting up to several days). This technique is useful for
isolating low-amplitude signals within data where background variability would
otherwise obscure detection. The application of composite analyses to
investigate the possible impacts of Fd events involves a statistical
examination of time-dependent atmospheric responses to Fds often from aerosol
and/or cloud datasets. Despite the publication of numerous results within this
field, clear conclusions have yet to be drawn and much ambiguity and
disagreement still remain. In this paper, we argue that the conflicting
findings of composite studies within this field relate to methodological
differences in the manner in which the composites have been constructed and
analyzed. Working from an example, we show how a composite may be objectively
constructed to maximize signal detection, robustly identify statistical
significance, and quantify the lower-limit uncertainty related to hypothesis
testing. Additionally, we also demonstrate how a seemingly significant false
positive may be obtained from non-significant data by minor alterations to
methodological approaches.
problem: Conflicting and ambiguous results from composite analyses studying the cosmic ray-cloud link stem from methodological inconsistencies in data filtering, normalization, and flawed statistical tests that often fail to properly assess significance, leading to unreliable conclusions and false positives.
method: The paper proposes a robust composite analysis methodology using Monte Carlo simulations to generate probability density functions from randomized data, providing an objective framework to construct composites, maximize signal detection, and robustly assess statistical significance without assumptions about the data's properties.
task: The task is to demonstrate a robust methodology for composite analysis of geophysical data using Monte Carlo methods to objectively construct composites, assess statistical significance, and avoid common pitfalls that lead to conflicting results and false positives.
innovation: This paper presents a robust methodology for composite analysis, using Monte Carlo simulations to objectively assess statistical significance and avoid false positives arising from common methodological errors in studies of solar-terrestrial relationships.

As an example, we will work from a composite of 44 Fd events identified from the Mt. Washington Observatory from 1984 to 1995, located at 44.30°N, 288.70°E, 1,900 m above mean sea level, at a cut-off rigidity of 1.24 GV (the list of Fd events were obtained from http://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/stp/ solar/cosmic.html).
